title: Batch vs Online Learning
abstract:
This is not a question about algorithms — it is a question about
how a model is trained and kept alive in production. Batch (offline)
learning trains once on the whole dataset and ships a frozen artefact; online
(incremental) learning keeps updating the same model as data arrives. This
document covers both, the concept drift that forces the choice, the
learning-rate dilemma that makes online learning genuinely hard, out-of-core
learning (which is about memory and is constantly confused with online
learning), and the production risks of each.

blocks.t: What This Distinction Is Actually About
Frame it correctly

Batch vs online describes how an ML model is trained and updated over
time in a production setup. It is orthogonal to supervised/unsupervised and
orthogonal to which algorithm you pick. The same logistic regression can be
trained in batch or online mode.

blocks.cap:
The two production topologies. In batch learning the arrow back to
 training is manual, periodic and expensive. In online learning it is automatic,
 continuous and cheap — which is both its strength and its danger.

blocks.t: Batch (Offline) Learning
The one-sentence version

The model is trained on the full dataset at once, locally, and then
deployed. It does not update again until you retrain it locally and deploy it
again.
The lifecycle is a loop that a human drives:

items: Collect all available data.
Train the model to convergence on all of it, offline.

Evaluate, then freeze the model into an artefact (a .pkl, an ONNX
 graph, a container).

Deploy. The artefact is now read-only — it serves predictions and learns
 nothing.
Wait days or weeks. Performance decays.
Go to step 1 with the newer data.

blocks.t: Why it is called "offline"

Not because the machine lacks internet, but because the learning happens
away from the live traffic. Serving and learning are two separate phases that
never overlap. Roughly 90% of deployed ML systems work this way, and for most
problems it is the correct choice.
Disadvantages of batch learning

items:
Every retrain uses the entire history, not just the
 new rows. After three years of logs, a nightly retrain means re-reading three
 years of data every night to learn about one day of it.

The full dataset must fit in memory (or you must
 reach for out-of-core methods, \S5). Training may need many CPU-hours or a GPU
 cluster; that cost recurs on every retrain.

There is a delay between the world changing and
 your model knowing about it. For a news recommender or a stock signal, a model
 that is one week stale is worthless.
Compute, storage, and the engineering time to run the pipeline.

blocks.t: The failure mode nobody warns you about

A batch model does not fail loudly. It degrades silently — the API keeps
returning 200 OK with confident-looking probabilities that are progressively
more wrong. Without a monitoring job comparing predictions against outcomes, you
will find out from a business stakeholder, not from your alerts.
Online (Incremental) Learning
The one-sentence version

The model updates itself continuously in production as new data comes
in, in small chunks, without retraining from scratch.

Data arrives as a stream. Each mini-batch (or even each single record) produces
a small update to the existing parameters. The model in production at 3pm is a
different model than the one at 2pm.
When you should use it

items:
The relationship between $X$ and $y$ is itself changing.
 This is the primary motivation — see \S3.2.

You never re-process the historical data. Update cost is
 proportional to new data, not all data. Old data can be deleted.

A new fraud pattern, a viral news topic, or a sudden
 demand shift is absorbed in minutes rather than at the next retrain.

Sensor telemetry, click logs, market ticks —
 data that never ends and could never be stored in full.

blocks.t: Concept drift — the thing online learning is for
Three ways a deployed model goes stale
Let the data be generated by $P_t(X,Y)$ at time $t$.

$$\textbf{Covariate shift:}&\quad P_t(X)\ \text{changes},\quad P_t(Y\mid X)\ \text{fixed}\\ \textbf{Prior / label shift:}&\quad P_t(Y)\ \text{changes},\quad P_t(X\mid Y)\ \text{fixed}\\ \textbf{Concept drift:}&\quad P_t(Y\mid X)\ \text{changes}$$

Only the third is true concept drift, and it is the dangerous one: the
rule itself has changed. A model trained on pre-pandemic mobility data
did not merely see new inputs — the mapping from inputs to outcomes had been
rewritten.

blocks.cap:
Three deployment strategies under drift. The never-retrained batch
 model decays monotonically. Scheduled retraining produces a sawtooth — it is
 always somewhat stale between retrains. Online learning tracks the change
 continuously.

blocks.t: The central challenge: the learning rate
The stability–plasticity dilemma

The learning rate $\eta$ controls how fast the online model learns, and
setting it correctly is the hard part of the whole approach:

items:
$\eta$ too high $\Rightarrow$ the model adapts to the newest data
 instantly and forgets everything it knew. A single hour of odd
 traffic destroys months of learning. This is
 catastrophic forgetting.

$\eta$ too low $\Rightarrow$ the model is stable but barely
 adapts — you have paid the complexity cost of online learning and got
 batch learning's staleness anyway.

blocks.t:
The business requirement is contradictory by nature: remember the old
stuff and learn the new stuff.

blocks.cap:
The same online update rule $w \leftarrow w + \eta(y-w)$ under three
 learning rates, with a genuine regime change at record 100. Low $\eta$ is
 smooth but lags badly; high $\eta$ tracks the change instantly but is dominated
 by noise.

blocks.t: Why the update rule is an exponential moving average
The simplest online update is
Unrolling it,

The weight on an observation $k$ steps ago decays as $(1-\eta)^k$. The
effective memory of the model is about $1/\eta$ observations. Setting
$\eta=0.01$ means "remember roughly the last 100 records". That is the concrete
meaning of choosing a learning rate.
Disadvantages of online learning

items:
You must tune $\eta$, monitor continuously, and version
 a model that changes every minute. Reproducing "the model that made
 yesterday's 4pm decision" requires replaying the exact stream.

Bad data goes straight into the live model with no human in the
 loop. A broken upstream ETL job, a sensor stuck at zero, or a deliberate
 data-poisoning attack corrupts production within minutes. Microsoft's
 Tay chatbot in 2016 is the textbook case: it learned from live user input and
 was made offensive within 24 hours.

There is no fixed test set. You need
 prequential evaluation — test on each record before training
 on it — plus rollback capability.

blocks.t: Guardrails are mandatory, not optional

Any real online system needs: input validation before the update, anomaly
detection on the incoming stream, a held-out canary set evaluated continuously,
a bound on how far parameters may move per window, and a snapshot to roll back
to. Without these, online learning is an unattended write path into production.
Out-of-Core Learning
The single most confused concept in this topic

Out-of-core learning is used when the data is too large to fit in
memory, so the model is trained in chunks instead of all at once.
It is about MEMORY only. It can be used with both online and
offline (batch) machine learning.

blocks.cap:
Out-of-core training reads the dataset in chunks that each fit in RAM
 and applies an incremental update per chunk. The mechanism resembles online
 learning — but the purpose is different.

head: Online learning
Out-of-core learning
rows: {Yes — they use the same partial_fit machinery}

blocks.t: The relationship in one sentence

Every online learner is necessarily out-of-core (a stream never fits in memory),
but an out-of-core learner need not be online — you can chunk through a 500 GB
file to produce one frozen batch model.
Side-by-Side Comparison

head: Dimension
Batch / Offline
Online / Incremental
rows: High, recurring, proportional to all data
Low, continuous, proportional to new data
Low; a human reviews each release
Stable domains: credit scoring, medical imaging, churn
Volatile domains: news feeds, fraud, ads, recommendations, IoT
\caption{Choosing between the two is a systems decision, not a modelling one.}

blocks.t: Code

# =====================================================================
# 1. BATCH LEARNING -- the ordinary case
# =====================================================================
import numpy as np, joblib
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = np.random.rand(50_000, 20), np.random.randint(0, 2, 50_000)

model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
model.fit(X, y)                    # sees ALL the data, once, to convergence
joblib.dump(model, "model_v1.pkl") # frozen artefact -> ships to production
# From here the model NEVER changes until a human retrains and redeploys.


# =====================================================================
# 2. ONLINE LEARNING -- partial_fit on a stream
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier

# eta0 is the learning rate: the stability/plasticity dial.
# learning_rate="constant" keeps it fixed so the model never stops adapting.
online = SGDClassifier(loss="log_loss", learning_rate="constant", eta0=0.01)

classes = np.array([0, 1])         # MUST be declared on the first call,
                                   # because a chunk may not contain every class

def stream_batches(n_batches=200, size=64):
    for _ in range(n_batches):
        yield np.random.rand(size, 20), np.random.randint(0, 2, size)

for Xb, yb in stream_batches():
    online.partial_fit(Xb, yb, classes=classes)   # one small update per chunk
# The model is different after every single line above.


# =====================================================================
# 3. PREQUENTIAL EVALUATION -- how you score an online model
# =====================================================================
correct = total = 0
for Xb, yb in stream_batches(50):
    if total:                                  # TEST first, on unseen data...
        correct += (online.predict(Xb) == yb).sum()
        total   += len(yb)
    else:
        total = len(yb)
    online.partial_fit(Xb, yb, classes=classes)  # ...THEN train on it
print("prequential accuracy:", correct / max(total, 1))


# =====================================================================
# 4. OUT-OF-CORE -- a 500 GB CSV, 8 GB of RAM
# =====================================================================
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDRegressor

model = SGDRegressor(learning_rate="invscaling", eta0=0.01)

for epoch in range(3):                          # several passes = still BATCH
    reader = pd.read_csv("huge.csv", chunksize=100_000)   # never loads it all
    for chunk in reader:
        Xc = chunk.drop(columns="target").values
        yc = chunk["target"].values
        model.partial_fit(Xc, yc)               # same API, different PURPOSE
# Goal here was MEMORY, not adaptation. The result is a frozen batch model.


# =====================================================================
# 5. GUARDRAILS -- what a real online system must add
# =====================================================================
import copy
snapshot   = copy.deepcopy(online)   # rollback point
canary_X, canary_y = np.random.rand(500, 20), np.random.randint(0, 2, 500)
BASELINE   = (online.predict(canary_X) == canary_y).mean()

for Xb, yb in stream_batches(100):
    # (a) validate the incoming chunk before letting it touch the model
    if np.isnan(Xb).any() or len(np.unique(yb)) == 0:
        continue                                       # drop bad chunk
    if np.abs(Xb).max() > 1e6:                         # sensor stuck / bad ETL
        continue

    online.partial_fit(Xb, yb, classes=classes)

    # (b) canary check -- has this update quietly broken the model?
    score = (online.predict(canary_X) == canary_y).mean()
    if score < BASELINE - 0.10:
        online = copy.deepcopy(snapshot)               # ROLL BACK
        print("update rejected, rolled back")
    else:
        snapshot = copy.deepcopy(online)               # accept as new baseline
Which estimators support partial_fit

Not all of them. In scikit-learn the incremental family includes
SGDClassifier, SGDRegressor, PassiveAggressive*,
Perceptron, MultinomialNB / BernoulliNB,
MiniBatchKMeans, IncrementalPCA and MiniBatchDictionaryLearning.
Tree ensembles such as RandomForestClassifier and XGBoost do
not support true incremental updates — a tree's structure cannot be
nudged by one record. For streaming trees you need Hoeffding trees
(the river library).
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
The distinction is about how the model is trained and updated in
 production, not about the algorithm.

Batch/offline: trained on the full dataset at once, deployed
 frozen, does not update until manually retrained. Disadvantages: lots of
 data, hardware limits, latency to adapt, cost.

Online: updates itself continuously in production as data
 arrives in chunks. Use it for concept drift, cost efficiency, and speed.

Concept drift means $P(Y\mid X)$ itself changed — the rule, not
 just the inputs. It is the reason online learning exists.

The learning rate is the central challenge: too high forgets the
 past, too low fails to learn the present. Effective memory $\approx 1/\eta$.

Out-of-core is about memory only — training in chunks
 because the data exceeds RAM. Usable with both online and offline setups.

Online learning's disadvantages are tricky and risky:
 bad data reaches production unsupervised. Guardrails are mandatory.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Is out-of-core learning the same as online learning?

No. Out-of-core solves a memory problem — the file is bigger than RAM,
so you stream it in chunks — and the result is usually a frozen batch model.
Online learning solves a time problem — the world is changing, so the
model must keep updating. They share the partial_fit mechanism, which is
why they are confused.

Q. Your fraud model's precision dropped from 0.91 to 0.68 over two
months. What happened and what do you do?

Almost certainly concept drift — fraudsters changed tactics, so
$P(Y\mid X)$ moved. Short term: retrain on recent data. Medium term: add drift
monitoring (population stability index on features, rolling performance on
delayed labels). Long term: move to online or frequently-scheduled retraining,
since fraud is adversarial and drift is permanent, not a one-off.

Q. Why is a high learning rate dangerous in online learning but often
fine in batch training?

In batch training you make many passes over a fixed dataset and can decay the
learning rate to convergence. In online learning there is one pass and no end;
a high constant rate means recent records permanently dominate, so the model's
effective memory shrinks to a handful of observations.
Q. How do you evaluate a model that changes every minute?

Prequential (interleaved test-then-train): for each incoming chunk, predict
first, record the error, then train on it. Complement this with a fixed canary
set and a rollback snapshot.
Q. Give a domain where batch learning is clearly correct.

Medical imaging diagnosis. The relationship between a tumour's appearance and
its malignancy does not drift week to week; regulatory approval requires a
fixed, auditable, reproducible artefact; and letting the model self-modify in
production would be unacceptable.
